_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Last lesson of the summer. Ole’s wheat came in dry, so you’re a hero. Don’t let it go to your hat.

replies.back: So it did. Then don’t let it go to your head.

replies.say: Thank you. I learned from the best.

turns.them: Now, the serious stuff. The county fair committee wants to know whether to hold the rodeo tomorrow afternoon if the heaps keep growing. And Ole’s threshing crew got caught out in a storm last week. They want to know when it’s safe to go back out after the thunder stops.

replies.back: Don’t sound so pleased. A storm doesn’t care how much you’ve studied.

replies.say: Can’t they just wait until it goes quiet?
replies.back: Quiet is the dangerous part. That’s what the crew learned. Nobody was hurt, thank heaven, but a bolt split the old cottonwood by Ole’s barn.

turns.them: This week: how a heap becomes a thunderstorm, how to count the distance to lightning, and a few rare clouds worth staying up for. Then one more when the autumn storms come, and you’re a qualified forecaster.

replies.back: Then we’ll see. There’s talk back East of fellows trying to make clouds rain on purpose. Probably nonsense. Probably.

turns.them: You’ve run one storm through its whole life. When does it throw its lightning and downpours?

replies.say: The mature stage, once the downdraught starts.
replies.back: Updraught and downdraught side by side. That’s when you want everybody under a roof.
Not yet. Growing, it’s all updraught. The trouble starts when rain and hail fall and drag a downdraught with them: the mature stage.
By then it’s raining itself out. The worst is the mature stage, with updraught and downdraught side by side.

turns.them: The rodeo committee will want a yes or a no, not a lecture. Practise saying no kindly.

replies.back: Now you’re thinking like a forecaster.

turns.them: Flash! Then thunder, nine seconds later. How far off?

replies.back: Nine divided by three. And that’s under thirty seconds, so everyone indoors.
Divide by three: about three kilometres. And under thirty seconds, so everyone indoors.
Three kilometres is close enough to be struck. Under thirty seconds, get indoors.

turns.them: Thirty minutes after the last thunder. Tell Ole’s crew I said so, and that I’ll hear about it if they don’t.

replies.say: How would you hear about it?
replies.back: Mabel at the switchboard. Mabel hears everything.

turns.them: That’s the last of the club’s photographs. Now the fair committee and Ole’s crew. Pass this and I’ll only call you tenderfoot on Sundays.

replies.say: And the rest of the week?
replies.back: Harrow. One more lesson, and I’ll mean it.
